title: Decluttering My Space
subtitle: One object at a time, and one question about each.
objectives: Define clutter and explain how it accumulates
Apply the keep or let go decision to a single object
Sort items into keep, donate, sell, recycle and bin
Explain why decluttering must come before organising
Explain why unwanted items must leave the room the same day

cards.title: Clutter is not mess. It is postponed decisions
cards.text: A pile is not dirty. It is a stack of things nobody has decided about yet, and it grows because deciding is the hard bit.

cards.title: Nothing arrives as clutter
cards.text: Everything came in as something useful, a gift, or a maybe. It becomes clutter by sitting undecided.
points: **Things arrive faster than they leave.**
**"I might need it"** is the phrase that does it.
**No decision is itself a decision** — to keep it.
**Which is why it never stops on its own.**

cards.title: Declutter first. Organise second
cards.text: Organising things you do not want is the most common mistake in this topic, and it wastes the whole afternoon.
points: **Tidy junk is still junk.**
**You are buying storage for things you will bin later.**
**Cut first, then arrange what is left.**
**It is much faster in that order.**

cards.title: One object, one question
cards.text: Tap through the four steps. This is the whole method.

question.text: What should you do before organising a space?
options: Declutter it, so you only organise what you are keeping
question.explain: Organising things you do not want wastes the effort. Cut first, then arrange what survives.

cards.title: One question, asked out loud
cards.text: Have I used this in the last year? Not might I, not could I. Have I.
points: **"Might I need it"** keeps everything. That is why it fails.
**Seasonal things** get judged over a whole year.
**If you cannot answer in five seconds**, that is an answer.
**One object at a time.** Never a whole pile.

cards.title: Death Stranding is a game about what to carry
cards.text: You cannot take everything. Every extra item costs balance and stamina, so you decide before you set off.
points: **Weight is the whole mechanic.**
**Leaving things behind is a skill** in it.
**A room has the same limit**, less obviously.
**Capacity is real** whether or not a bar shows it.

question.text: Which question sorts an object fastest?
options: Have I used this in the last year?
question.explain: Have I, not might I. Might I keeps everything, which is exactly why nothing gets sorted.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: The decision is made. Part 2 is what happens to everything you did not keep. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Deciding is only half the job
cards.text: A bag you decided to let go, still in the corner on Friday, is just clutter in a bag.

cards.title: Not everything goes in the bin
cards.text: Sorting the outgoing pile properly is part of the skill, and most of it never needs to reach a landfill.
points: **Keep** — it has a home to go to.
**Donate** — usable, and someone else needs it.
**Sell** — worth the effort of listing it.
**Recycle or bin** — genuinely finished.

cards.title: A workshop has a parts bin and a scrap bin
cards.text: They are never the same bin. Sorting on the way out is what stops a garage filling up with things nobody will ever use.
points: **Good parts get kept and labelled.**
**Scrap leaves the building.**
**A pile that is neither** grows forever.
**Decide at the moment you take it off.**

cards.title: Out of the room the same day
cards.text: Anything you decided to let go has to physically leave, today. Otherwise it quietly moves back in.
points: **Bags by the door**, not under the bed.
**In the car, or in the bin, today.**
**A donation bag left for a week** gets unpacked.
**The decision only counts** once it leaves.

question.text: Why must let-go items leave the room the same day?
options: Otherwise they get unpacked and quietly move back in
question.explain: A bag left in the corner is still clutter. The decision only counts once the item is gone.

cards.title: Kit that does not fit is not kit
cards.text: Old wraps, split gloves, shoes you grew out of. They take space in the bag and none of them are usable.
points: **Grown out of** is the easiest possible decision.
**Split or worn gear** is a safety question too.
**A lighter bag** gets carried more often.
**Do it once a term.** It takes ten minutes.

question.text: You should organise a room first, then decide what to get rid of.
question.explain: False. Declutter first. Organising things you are about to throw away wastes the whole effort.

terms.def: Objects nobody has decided about yet. Postponed decisions, not dirt.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Clutter is postponed decisions**, not dirt.
**Declutter first, organise second.**
**Have I used it in a year?** One object at a time.
**It leaves the room today**, or it comes back.

options: Objects nobody has decided about yet
Dirt and dust in a room
Things that belong to someone else
quiz.explain: Postponed decisions. That is why it grows: not deciding is itself a decision to keep.
quiz.objective: Define clutter and explain how it accumulates

quiz.text: Why does clutter build up on its own?
options: Things arrive faster than decisions get made about them
It only happens in untidy homes
quiz.explain: Nothing arrives as clutter. It becomes clutter by sitting undecided.
quiz.objective: Define clutter and explain how it accumulates

quiz.text: Which question should you ask about each object?
options: Have I used this in the last year?
Might I need this one day?
quiz.explain: Have I, not might I. The might-I question keeps everything, which is why it fails.
quiz.objective: Apply the keep or let go decision to a single object

quiz.text: You should sort a whole pile at once rather than one object at a time.
quiz.explain: False. Facing a whole pile is what makes people stop. One object, one question, then the next.
quiz.objective: Apply the keep or let go decision to a single object

quiz.text: You have a jacket that still fits and is in good condition, but you never wear it. Best outcome?
options: Put it back in the wardrobe
quiz.explain: Usable and unwanted is exactly the donate pile. Very little needs to reach a landfill.
quiz.objective: Sort items into keep, donate, sell, recycle and bin

quiz.text: Put the decluttering process in the right order.
items: Ask if you have used it in a year
Sort it into keep or let go
Take the let-go bag out of the room
quiz.explain: One object, one question, one destination, and then it physically leaves the same day.
quiz.objective: Apply the keep or let go decision to a single object

quiz.text: Why should you declutter before organising?
options: Organising things you are about to get rid of wastes the effort
It makes the room look bigger first
quiz.explain: Tidy junk is still junk. Cut first, then arrange what is left. It is much faster that way round.
quiz.objective: Explain why decluttering must come before organising

quiz.text: Buying storage boxes is a good first step in decluttering.
quiz.explain: False. That is buying homes for things you have not decided to keep. Decide first.
quiz.objective: Explain why decluttering must come before organising

quiz.text: Why must let-go items leave the room the same day?
options: A bag left in the corner gets unpacked and moves back in
So you can measure the space
quiz.explain: The decision only counts once the item is actually gone. Bags by the door, not under the bed.
quiz.objective: Explain why unwanted items must leave the room the same day

quiz.text: Which item belongs in the recycle or bin pile rather than donate?
options: A pair of gloves that has split open
A shirt you have grown out of
A game you no longer play
quiz.explain: Split gear is finished and unsafe to pass on. The other three are still usable by somebody.
quiz.objective: Sort items into keep, donate, sell, recycle and bin

quiz.text: What happens if you keep everything you might need one day?
options: Nothing ever leaves, so the total only grows
You save money in the long run
quiz.explain: Might-I keeps everything by design. That is why the one-year question is asked instead.
quiz.objective: Define clutter and explain how it accumulates

quiz.text: Not making a decision about an object is the same as deciding to keep it.
quiz.explain: True, and that is exactly how clutter accumulates without anyone choosing it.

teacher.summary: Week 3 TLE covers decluttering, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The definition it opens with does the heavy lifting: clutter is postponed decisions rather than dirt, which reframes the whole task as decision-making and explains why it accumulates without anyone choosing it. The sortFlow figure holds the method to one object and one question, because facing a whole pile is what makes people stop — which is worth knowing for any learner, and particularly for this one. Two rules are given more weight than the rest: declutter before organising, since organising things you are about to discard wastes the afternoon; and the same-day rule, since a decision that does not result in the item leaving is not a decision at all.
discussion: Ask him what 'I might need it' has ever actually saved. The honest answer usually settles the question.
Ask why deciding about a whole pile is harder than deciding about one object. It is the same reason a big task is harder to start than a small one.
Ask what should happen to a bag of donations. The same-day rule only means something if somebody drives it somewhere.
Ask whether decluttering is about having less or about deciding faster. Both answers are defensible.
teacher.extension: Set a timer for ten minutes and have him run the flow on one drawer, out loud. Saying the question aloud for each object is what makes the method stick, and ten minutes is enough to prove it works.
misconceptions: 'Clutter is mess.' A pile can be perfectly clean. Clutter is a stack of undecided objects.
'Organise first, then get rid of things.' The other way round. Tidy junk is still junk.
'The right question is might I need this.' That question keeps everything. Ask whether you have used it in a year.
'Deciding to let something go is the end of the job.' It has to leave the room the same day, or it comes back.
